prompt: On a scatter plot of price against units sold, the points fall from left to right. What does that describe?
hint: Which way do the points slope?

choices.why: Positive means the points rise: both go up together.
Right. As one goes up, the other tends to go down.
Variation is what makes a pattern visible at all.

choices.text: Proof that price causes the sales
choices.why: A scatter plot shows association; cause is lesson 18.

prompt: Put the four things to read in a scatter plot in the order this lesson gives them.
hint: Which way first, then what shape.

prompt: Horta plots distance and minutes for its deliveries. Which goes on the horizontal axis, and why?
hint: Which one could plausibly influence the other?

choices.text: Minutes, because it was measured first
choices.why: The order of measurement does not decide the axes.

choices.text: Either, and r would change with the choice
choices.why: Swapping axes leaves r unchanged; the convention is about reading.
Size of values has nothing to do with it.
Right. The variable that might influence the other goes across, by convention.

prompt: The twelve orders have covariance 248.77 between items and basket, and standard deviations of 4.20 items and R$ 59.42. What is r? Give three decimal places.
hint: Covariance ÷ (s of x × s of y).

prompt: The products of deviations for twelve orders add up to 2,736.49. What is the sample covariance? Give two decimal places.
Horta re-records every basket in cents instead of reais. What happens to the correlation between items and basket?
hint: What does dividing by the two standard deviations remove?

choices.why: Right. r has no units, so rescaling either variable leaves it unchanged.

choices.text: It becomes a hundred times larger
choices.why: That happens to the covariance, not to r.

choices.text: It becomes a hundred times smaller
choices.why: Dividing by the standard deviations cancels the unit.
Rescaling by a positive number keeps the direction.

prompt: A correlation is r = 0.7. What share of the variation do the two variables share, as r²? Give two decimal places.
Which correlation describes the tightest straight-line pattern?

choices.why: Weaker than 0.85 in size, whatever the sign.
Close to no straight-line trend.
Right. The size measures tightness; the sign is only direction.
Smaller in size than −0.85.

prompt: Write the t statistic for testing whether a correlation r, on n pairs, could be zero in the population.
hint: n − 2 under one root, 1 − r² under the other.

prompt: For 120 deliveries, items and minutes have r = 0.20 and p = 0.032. Which reading is right?
hint: Square r, and remember what p does not measure.

choices.text: Items explain 20% of the delivery times
choices.why: The share is r², 0.04, about 4%.

choices.text: Since p < 0.05, the link is strong
choices.why: A small p says it is probably not zero, not that it is strong.
Right. Probably not chance, and of little use for any one delivery.
p = 0.032 makes chance an unlikely explanation.

prompt: Anscombe's four data sets all have r = 0.816. What do they show?

choices.text: That one r fits very different pictures
choices.why: Right. A curve, a line with a stray point and a lone lever all share it.

choices.text: That r = 0.816 means a strong straight line
choices.why: Only set I is a straight-line cloud.

choices.text: That small data sets give the wrong r
choices.why: Each r is computed correctly; it just cannot see the shape.

choices.text: That Pearson's r is a broken measure
choices.why: It measures straight-line fit, and that is all it claims.

prompt: For x from −5 to 5 and y = x², Pearson's r is 0. What does that say?

choices.text: y does not depend on x
choices.why: y depends on x exactly; the dependence is not a straight line.
It is correct: the two halves cancel.
The curve turns back, so the ranks do not agree either; rho is 0 too.
Right. A perfect relationship can have r = 0 when it turns back on itself.

prompt: Rank the values 12, 7, 30, 7 from smallest, giving tied values the average of their ranks. What rank do the two 7s each get?
Weekly orders rise with every extra point of discount, but less each time. Pearson's r is 0.85. What is Spearman's?
hint: Does y ever go down as x goes up?

choices.why: Ranks ignore the bend, so the agreement is perfect.
Right. Every rise in x brings a rise in y, so the ranks agree completely.
They match only when the relationship is a straight line.
It flattens but never turns back.

prompt: When is Spearman's coefficient the better choice than Pearson's? Choose all that apply.
hint: What do ranks keep, and what do they throw away?

choices.why: Yes: ratings have order but no reliable distances.

choices.text: The relationship curves but keeps rising
choices.why: Yes: ranks capture a monotonic curve in full.

choices.text: The relationship rises and then falls
choices.why: Ranks miss that too; draw it instead.

choices.text: One or two values are extreme
choices.why: Yes: a rank cannot be further than the top.

prompt: Ten deliveries show no pattern, r = −0.17. One added point far away makes r = 0.96. Spearman's for the eleven is 0.14. Why so different?
hint: How far can a rank be from the others?

choices.why: It uses every point, ranked.

choices.text: To ranks it is only the top value
choices.why: Right. Ranks cap its pull, so the ten patternless points still dominate.
The arithmetic is right; the point really dominates the products.

choices.text: Eleven points are too few for Pearson's
choices.why: Both coefficients use the same eleven points.

prompt: Across 120 deliveries, distance and minutes have r = 0.91. For Centro and Cambuí alone, r = 0.37. What explains the drop?
hint: How wide is the window of distances?

choices.text: Distance matters less near the warehouse
choices.why: Each kilometre still adds a little over two minutes there.

choices.text: Sixty deliveries are too few to measure r
choices.why: Sixty is plenty; the range is the issue.

choices.text: The two neighbourhoods have more outliers
choices.why: Neither shows a point far from the rest.
Right. Over three kilometres, the noise is as large as the effect.

prompt: A correlation coefficient always lies between ___ and ___.
hint: A perfect falling line and a perfect rising one.

prompt: A sample of 27 pairs gives r = 0.5. What is the t statistic for testing whether the population correlation is zero? Give two decimal places.
Match each situation to what it does to a correlation.
hint: Think of the lever, the window, the parabola and the units.

pairs.left: One point far from a patternless cluster
Measuring only a narrow range of x
A curve that rises then falls
